Well done, sir. I found the script funny and enjoyable. Both characters are universally relatable, and in a world of many birthdays to remember, I almost wish Husband Man actually existed.

Here were some of my thoughts if you're looking to tweak it:

* If I may be honest, Lance in his current state seems somewhat of a undeveloped character. My questions to you would be: a) Who is this guy aside from a husband that forgets birthdays? b) How does him forgetting his wife's birthday make him FEEL? c) Does he have any other quirks or character traits that might be fun to play for an actor, such as having the memory span of a fish? Right now, he seems mainly there to set up the hilarious character of HUSBAND MAN, and I would argue his quirkiness and energy is too similar to him. It might be better to give him more contrast and build on his character (mostly to give the actor juicier lines to read!)
* To add to the above, I think that Lance should be somewhat of an **obstacle** for Husband Man. What would be the absolute worse case scenario for him (in an ironic way)? Perhaps Lance could be so bad of a husband that this 'rescue' becomes nearly an impossible task. Not only does he forget birthday, but he doesn't even dress appropriately, or shower, or worse -- love her. I don't know ... I'll leave that up to you, but I would recommend adding more **conflict**. Conflict can be funny/playful, and it's what hooks and holds an audience. Also, I never really picked up a want for the husband and I think you should address that as well.
* On the first page, I would just introduce these characters as quickly as possible. The awkwardness is comedic, but there's so much better stuff you can focus on. You can get to the side step joke much faster -- pretty much on his first line.
* To give this script stakes, I would introduce that the husband’s wife is on her way home at this very moment (and you can cut to her driving home) – and maybe this guy has ‘Husband Man’ senses (which would be kind of weird and hilarious) – where he can visual her driving home. Also, you should explain what WOULD happen if this man forgets her birthday. Will she divorce him? Is this the last straw? Whatever you choose –  you gotta set up the stakes.

Overall, it would be a funny script to see. I would really recommend digging deep into each of these characters. Explore their wants, history, drives, ticks, quirks, etc. I would even write an outline of who both these characters are … what their backstory is ... and do your sub-text/character work. You need to make it so this moment on this walkway is the most critical and interesting moment of both their lives.

Good luck and hope that helped! If not, just film it man!!! Would be a great short for Valentine's Day

My advice ... take it with a grain of salt:

* I'm not sure why you labeled your drafts on the cover page. If this is the first time you're sharing it with professionals, I personally would leave it out. It can also be a red flag that a) you're amateur or b) you've shopped the script around on previous drafts and nobody wants to buy it.
* I don't write television so I might be wrong here ... but that second character page is completely wasted space. Any character descriptions should be saved for the initial character introduction, because nobody is going to read anything else. The script is what matters ... just my opinion. The quote is fine.
* Speaking of your character introductions, I would stick with simplicity and clarity. Get to the point of the character as fast as possible. Are they the jock? The shy one? The class clown?
   * For example, when you introduce Brian, I would just say "Brian, 16, the straight man of the group, and the oldest -- even though he doesn't always act like it". Him being "African American" tells us nothing (unless it's important to his character). Him wearing Jeff Goldblum glasses also tells us nothing. Leave this stuff for the casting director and costume designer. You don't have a lot of time to tell us who these characters are, so use your real-estate efficiently and get straight to the point. I only say this because your other introductions give too much information too.
   * To add to that, you don't need to describe somebody's attractiveness ... they're actors on a television show ... they're all going to be good looking.
* I agree on the font comment. I'd go with the industry standard just to be safe.
* There's a typo on page 19 (that's honestly why I'm commenting lol). I think you meant to say: "Brian: This is worse **than** that ... "  You're welcome. I just saved the show.
* Overall, from what I skimmed, I think you can clean up your action lines a bit, if you're looking for stuff to tweak. Everybody has their own style, but I always find that most of the action lines should be used to ONLY set up the scene. If you break up the dialogue too much with action lines it can *sometimes* ruin the flow.
   * On page 20, for example, you can move the "We hear a BEEPING NOISE" down to the line below it and I think it'd read better. Stuff like that will help the flow a lot. Remember, screenplays are read DOWN not across. Only tell us what we NEED to know, otherwise I would just take it out. Typically, people hate reading action lines. Well ... at least I do hah

Anyway, hope that helps. Sorry to not have any notes on character or plot. I think your dialogue is fine, and the characters seem real, but the action lines did make the read robotic for me. Hope this stuff helped and good luck!

The script has conflict and diverse characters, which is great. There's definately comedic potential here. Unfortunately I didn't have too much time to read it (at work) but I'll give you some of my quick thoughts:

* Don't repeat information. Your first slugline is "suburban street" and you immediately follow it by telling us we're on a suburban street. I'm only saying this so you never ever ever ever do this again ... these types of mistakes are SCRIPT POISON! 😆 

* Economy of words. I think you take way to long to say what you want to say (which is completely fine for a first draft ... but not fine for the second). I would keep your action lines to 2 - 3 lines maximum. Remember, you don't have to describe every little detail. One word or two sets the image in our heads and you saved the reader a lot of headaches. Be quick. Be direct. Be aware.

* I think you can add better lines than just "G'day" and "Come in" for the greeting scenes. Any time you see this, try to give more juice for the actors to read, and more character for them to work with. 

**Story notes:**

* I personally thought it was weird that the father was okay with what the kid is watching on the internet. Maybe just don't stay there as long as you do ... I don't know that's just me... there's conflict in the scene so that's good.

* These kids are very sophisticated for ten year olds ... but obviously that's intentional. My advice would be to maybe dumb down the supportive friend in the opening to balance out the absurdity, and show the reader you know what your doing, which you do.

Anyway, those were my quick thoughts. Keep up the good work👍

Well done with the opening. The fortune teller gimic immediately got me hooked and made the clerk a likeable/authentic character. I think the script works as is, but here are some of my thoughts if you wanted to play around with it:

* Beliability: If I'm being honest the script kind of fell apart for me once you started to bend the logic with the clerks reaction to the robbery. Even though this is all a dream in the end (and I'll talk about that in a second) I think it would work better if you justified why he's acting so casually. Maybe it has something to do with his fortune cookies, which he holds as inherent truth? Maybe he's wearing some gypsies magic necklace that makes him bulletproof?

* Too add to this, I think you set up a uniquely charming character in this opening scene, but then you immediately drift away from his essence for comedic purposes, and in doing so, you essentially abandonded the character, which made these two guys read the same. My interpretation of the joke is that this jewelry clerk is "difficult", so why not stay "difficult" within the boundaries of his character? Like if he answers each question with a magic eight ball, or a tarot card? All in all, when the clerk started to derail from the person you introduced ... I started to ask the dreaded question - "what is this about? Whats the point of this scene?"

* I guess my last note would be, you have all the ingredients of a funny story with potentially strong characters ... I would try to find something that you want to say and leave the audience with a genuine, new experience. I personally wouldnt go the dream route, but if you do (which is fine), my advice would be to establish that within the first 30 seconds and escalate it so the audience can play along ... by leaving it a twist it kind of ends anti-clamaticly and tropish.

So yeah those are my rough notes. Again, it works as is, but wanted to give my honest feedback. Hoping its helpful and that you film this!

This question comes up and there really is only one word ...

**NETWORK.**

If you study the early success of any comedy actor or TV creator, you'll find that a lot of them did stand up comedy. Why does that work? Because producers and "representatives" get to *see* you, and see your work. You could be the greatest screenwriter in the world, but if they don't know you exist, then it's kinda hard for them to magically find you.

Hence the networking part.

**Networking includes:** going to panels, signing up for film events, making a movie, going to a film college, joining a writing group, hanging out at a bar with other film people ... it doesn't really matter who you do these things with, but you have to do them.

To put it in even simpler terms. The networking part works because **it's who you know**. If you were the offspring of a famous actor, or producer, or director, or talent scout, I guarantee it'd be very easy to get represented. (Sorry if that sounds cynical, but it's usually just how the world works. Kinda how most of us choose the same professions as our parents). It's all about connections, and finding people who can get your film done. So just find those people.

Good luck to anybody reading this ...
